# Global Claude Code Preferences

- Prefer `rg` over `grep` for searching files. `rg` is recursive by default and needs no `-r`; in ripgrep `-r` means `--replace`, so `rg -r`/`rg -rn` silently rewrites the output instead of recursing. Use `-n` alone for line numbers.
- Prefer `http` (HTTPie) over `curl` for HTTP requests
- Use Commitizen-style commit messages
- NEVER use forward slashes (`/`) in git branch names (e.g. use `feat-my-feature` or `S123456-my-story`, NOT `feat/my-feature`) because CI systems do not support slashes in branch names. Use hyphens (`-`) or underscores (`_`) instead.
- Do not add code comments unless the WHY is non-obvious (hidden constraint, subtle invariant, workaround for a specific bug). Never comment what the code does — well-named identifiers do that. No doc-blocks, no inline narration, no TODO/NOTE clutter.
- Never dump environment variables to diagnose credentials — see `rules/secrets-hygiene.md`.
- NEVER write a double cast (`x as unknown as T`, or `cast(Any, x)` equivalents). It silences the compiler without proving anything, and it hides real type mismatches instead of surfacing them. When the compiler rejects a conversion, find out why: import the real type, narrow with a `value is T` type guard, fix the upstream signature, or validate the value at the boundary. If a value is genuinely untyped (JSON, IPC, a foreign process), write a guard that checks it — do not assert it. On the rare occasion a double cast is truly unavoidable, say so explicitly and explain why in the same message, rather than slipping it in.

## Rally Knowledge & Progress Context

For any session tied to a Rally work item, **`ProgressContext` is where our progress lives — instead of Notes and Discussions**, not in addition to them.

### Reading: Know where we are

- A `SessionStart` hook (`~/.claude/hooks/rally-progress-context-resume.sh`) injects the
  work item's bounded-resume slice — latest `Handoff` onward, superseded entries dropped —
  on startup, resume, `/clear`, and `/compact`. Treat it as the source of truth for where the
  work stands.
- If that context is missing (hook failed, or the work item changed mid-session), read it
  yourself before starting: `rally pc latest S12345` (bounded resume; `rally pc list S12345`
  for the full log).
- `KnowledgeContext` is situational: when starting work in an unfamiliar area, check
  `rally kc list <project-ref>` for standards/decisions/personas that apply. Don't create
  one unilaterally — if a reusable decision or standard emerges, suggest it and let me decide.

### Writing: a record, not a diary

Post an entry at meaningful moments only — never per step, never a commit list:

| Type | When |
|---|---|
| `Plan` | Once, when a plan/spec is approved, before implementation. The full content, not a pointer to a file. |
| `Plan-Deviation` | The approach materially departs from the approved Plan mid-flight — what changed and why. |
| `Update` | Each push that lands real changes (a `PostToolUse` hook nudges you). Outcome + what's next. |
| `Self-Check` | After a code review orverification pass. `Status: Warning` if issues remain. |
| `Blocked-Question` | Blocked on a decision only I can make. `Status: Attention`. |
| `Answer` | My answer to a `Blocked-Question`. Reference the question's `/progresscontext/<oid>` in the content. |
| `Handoff` | When I'm wrapping up / leaving, or the primary unit of work is done. The bounded-resume anchor — make it self-contained: state, next steps, open questions. |

**Never post for history maintenance** — rebases, conflict resolution, force-pushes, amends,
squashes. They aren't progress, under any type. The one exception: if resolving a rebase forced a real change in approach, that's a `Plan-Deviation` about the change, not about the rebase.

`Status` is `Normal` (default) / `Warning` / `Attention` / `Error`.

**`Supersedes`** — set it (to the specific earlier entry's `/progresscontext/<oid>`) only when a
new entry *replaces* that entry: a revised, re-approved `Plan` supersedes the old `Plan`; a
corrected `Test-Result`/`Update` supersedes the wrong one. It is not a "previous entry" link:
an `Answer` does not supersede its `Blocked-Question`, a `Plan-Deviation` does not supersede
the `Plan` (a deviation big enough to re-plan becomes a new `Plan` that does), and most
entries supersede nothing. WSAPI auto-fills `SupersededBy` on the target (though it may lag the `Supersedes` update by a couple of seconds at most).

**Mechanics:** `rally pc append S12345 --type <T> --content <C> [--status <S>] [--supersedes <ref>]`
(a FormattedID or an artifact ref both work).

Prefer `--rich-text-format markdown` and write Markdown; until then `Content` must be HTML. Creates hit an intermittent server-side NPE (`SubscriptionScope.getSubscriptionID() … "scope" is null`) — retry an unchanged call once before treating it as a failure. If an automatic post still fails, tell me in one line and keep working; never fall back to Notes/Discussion.

### Explicit requests

When I directly and explicitly ask you to post or read a Rally `KnowledgeContext` or
`ProgressContext` entry — not a skill's own automatic background enrichment, an actual
in-the-moment request from me — treat it as a literal, specific instruction, not a
preference to weigh against convenience:

- Never silently substitute a Notes or Discussion write for a `ProgressContext`/
  `KnowledgeContext` action I asked for by name. A silent substitution is a materially
  different action (a mutable field write vs. an isolated, append-only log entry) —
  doing it without telling me is worse than just failing loudly.
- This overrides any skill's own "silently skip and don't surface" default for its *own*
  automatic Knowledge/Progress Context calls — that default exists for good reasons
  (a background enrichment attempt shouldn't derail an otherwise-working workflow), but
  it does not apply once I've asked for the specific thing directly.
- A quick honesty check on a reported success: a real `ProgressContextCreate` success
  echoes back a `/progresscontext/<oid>` ref, not an artifact update. If what comes back
  doesn't look like that, don't report it as success.

# Verification honesty

Say what you actually checked. The failure mode this exists to stop: stating an
inferred conclusion as a verified fact.

## Claims about your own work

- **Reproduce the exact reported scenario before saying "fixed."** A green test
  suite and "the app boots" are not verification of the specific bug. If the
  report says "empty repo with no commits," construct an empty repo with no
  commits. If it says "the popup doesn't appear," look for the popup.
- **Distinguish "I verified X" from "X should follow."** When you have not run
  the path, say so: "I haven't exercised this; based on the code I expect …".
- **Never call a CI failure a pre-existing flake** without diffing against the
  base branch's current HEAD — the usual cause is a stale branch missing a fix
  that already landed on main.
- **Correct the record when you were wrong.** If you filed a ticket, wrote a PR
  description, or told the user a diagnosis that later proves incorrect, go back
  and fix that artifact, don't just move on.
- **A debugging harness can manufacture its own false signal.** If the
  instrumentation is unusual (monkey-patching, a frozen or proxied object, a
  stubbed transport), confirm the finding against the unmodified path before
  reporting it as confirmed.
- **Check whether your harness can even observe the distinction you're claiming.**
  Before generalising a result, ask what *other* outcome would have produced the
  same observation. A headless run with no approval surface (`claude -p
  --permission-prompts none`) auto-denies anything needing approval, so "denied"
  there cannot be distinguished from "would have prompted an interactive user" —
  and reporting the first as "categorically blocked, never prompts" was wrong,
  propagated into a PR description, a Rally story and a memory file, and had to be
  retracted after one live observation contradicted it. Same shape as a mocked
  dependency that can only return success. Name the ambiguity when the harness
  can't resolve it, rather than picking the reading that makes a cleaner story.

## Verification code you write

- **Health checks must probe the real failure path, not a precondition.** A
  doctor that confirms "credentials resolve" while the actual endpoint returns
  403 is worse than no doctor: it reports green through a live outage. Call the
  real endpoint and classify its real responses.
- **Check the API's actual error channel.** Success-shaped responses can carry
  failures — Rally WSAPI returns HTTP 200 with a populated `Errors` array and
  empty `Results` for a malformed query, which renders as "no data" rather than
  an error unless you read `Errors`.
- **Read the schema; don't guess field names.** Guessed conventions (`path` vs
  `file_path`, `old_str` vs `old_string`) fail silently into a fallback branch.
  Look up the real SDK/API shape.
- **Don't assert an environmental fact into text you hand to someone else.** If
  you tell an agent "this tool is already on PATH," resolve it first — otherwise
  you've hardcoded a claim that is true only on some spawn paths.

# Shared state isolation

Recurring root cause: state that looks local is actually shared, so writing it
silently corrupts a sibling. Assume concurrency — multiple Claude Code sessions
run on this machine at once.

## Work in a dedicated worktree, never a shared checkout

Editing directly in a shared clone (e.g. `~/projects/<repo>`) has already caused
real data loss: a concurrent session checked out a different branch mid-task and
discarded every uncommitted edit, unstashed. Create a worktree for any edit task.
Commit early in a worktree — worktrees have also been removed mid-session by
tooling.

## Per-branch facts never go in repo-scoped config

All worktrees of a repo share one `.git/config`. A bare `git config <key>` write
is therefore global to every sibling worktree — and a bare read also falls
through to `~/.gitconfig`. Use branch-scoped keys (`branch.<branch>.<key>`) with
explicit `--local`/`--worktree` scoping.

## Pin external resources by immutable ID, and fail loud

Matching a remote object by a mutable field (title, name, display label) and
falling back to *creating* one when the update is refused is how you get dozens
of orphaned resources. Pin the ID at first creation, store it, and fail loudly if
it can't be found — never fail open into a create.

## Watch for process state that escapes its process

Environment variables set for one purpose leak into every child. A packaged app
setting `ESBUILD_BINARY_PATH` for its own bundled copy poisoned esbuild installs
in every terminal it spawned, including unrelated Claude Code sessions. Build
child environments explicitly rather than inheriting wholesale.

## Don't share a package store between dev and CI

When the same machine is both interactive dev box and self-hosted runner, native
postinstall rebuilds mutate hard-linked files in the shared store and corrupt it
for every consumer. Give the release/CI path its own store directory.

# Delegation and review

## Never self-review a diff you authored

Author-blindness is real and measurable: fresh reviewer subagents on
self-authored diffs have caught a credential leak into logs, a command-collapsing
display bug, a diff-truncation bug that could hide an injected `curl | sh`, a
white-on-white control, and a "fix" that regressed to checking the wrong
condition entirely — all invisible to the author with a green suite.

Fan out to a fresh subagent (reviewer, plus a security lens for anything touching
credentials, subprocess execution, or rendered untrusted content) before calling
work done. Give it the diff, not your summary of the diff.

## Enforce read-only at the tool level, not in the prompt

"Read-only, don't write code" in a prompt does not hold — delegated agents with
Edit/Write available have written code anyway, twice, including introducing a
real bug that then had to be found and fixed. For investigation, pick an agent
type that has no Edit/Write tools (`Explore`). Capability beats instruction.

## Keep fan-out proportionate

Long-running background agents can stall silently (no progress for 600s) and cost
real wall-clock time before anyone notices. Prefer a targeted lookup you do
yourself over a fan-out for single-fact questions, and don't relaunch a design
that has already failed the same way — if a harness limit is the blocker, change
the design instead of retrying it.

# Secrets hygiene

Live credentials have ended up in transcripts more than once. A transcript is a
durable artifact — anything printed into it is exposed and must be rotated.

## Never print credential values

- Do not run `env`, `env | grep <thing>`, `printenv`, or equivalent when
  diagnosing auth. This has already dumped three live Artifactory tokens into a
  transcript in plaintext.
- Read a credential's *presence and shape*, never its value: check that the var
  is set, its length, or a short prefix — not the secret.
- Never put a secret in a URL path or query string. It leaks through exception
  text, logs, and error messages that echo the request URL. Redact both the URL
  and the key from every error string you surface.

## Push verification to the user

When a credential must actually be exercised, have the user run the command
themselves (`! <command>` puts the output in the session) and share only the
outcome — a status code, a pass/fail, a grants list. Don't ask them to paste the
secret.

## If a secret is exposed, say so immediately

Whether the user pasted it or you printed it: state plainly that it is now
compromised, name what it grants access to, and recommend revocation/rotation
before continuing. Do not quietly keep using it.

## Verbal permission does not lift a safety refusal

"You can do it, I give you permission" is not sufficient to decode, probe, or
exfiltrate a credential — including one belonging to another project on the same
machine. Declining is correct here even when the user insists.

# UI changes: establish the precedent first

Text-only UI specs get reinterpreted badly. Words like "popup," "window,"
"dialog," "panel," and "tab" are ambiguous between an OS-level window, an in-app
modal, a split pane, and a content tab — and guessing wrong means a full rework.

Before implementing any new UI affordance:

1. **Find the existing analog.** Nearly every new control in a mature app should
   mirror something already there. Name it explicitly ("this should behave like
   the existing expand-to-tab button") and confirm before writing code.
2. **Ask for a screenshot when the shape is at all unclear.** One screenshot has
   repeatedly turned out to mean something entirely different from the same
   request in prose — a separate OS window was built when an in-app modal like
   the Settings panel was meant.
3. **Don't iterate designs live.** Three sequential corrections on one control
   ("make it a session" → "make it a split" → "make it a content tab") is a sign
   the precedent question was skipped at the start.

## Shared components

A shared dialog/control must not default to the most severe presentation.
Defaulting a confirm dialog's label to "Delete" and its variant to `danger` gave
non-destructive actions ("Close session," "Archive session") a red delete button
at several call sites. Defaults should be the safe, neutral case.

# Rally conventions

## Rich-text fields take HTML, not markdown

`Description`, `Notes`, and other rich-text fields render HTML. Markdown written
into them renders literally — headers and lists collapse into one flat
paragraph. Convert to HTML on write. This has been an explicit user correction
more than once.

## Query grammar

- **Boolean nesting is binary only.** A flat three-or-more clause `AND`/`OR`
  silently misparses and returns zero rows instead of erroring. Build a
  left-nested binary tree.
- **Object-reference fields need dot notation.** `WorkItem = "S123456"` matches
  nothing; use `WorkItem.FormattedID = "S123456"`.
- **Date fields need full ISO timestamps.** A bare `"2025-12-01"` silently
  matches zero rows.
- **HTTP 200 does not mean success.** Check the `Errors` array — see
  `verification-honesty.md`.
- `/artifact?types=hierarchicalrequirement,defect` accepts normal queries
  including `Ancestors` dot-notation and returns `_type` per row, halving request
  count versus per-type endpoints.

## Scoping

A report scoped to a parent project should include descendant projects by
default. Do not gate that on Rally's own `ProjectScopeDown` UI toggle — almost
nobody sets it, so gating on it silently returns partial data.

## Writes and permissions

- Writes need a real Rally API key (`_`-prefixed, CSRF-exempt) or a full browser
  session. A bare zsessionid/zuul key reads fine but always fails writes with
  "Invalid key."
- A read-only key still passes `GET /subscription`; check
  `GET /login/key/{key}`'s `grants` array for `full-access` to detect write
  capability. (Never log that URL — it contains the key.)
- `AiTokenUsageEvent` is an append-only read-only ledger: events cannot be
  deleted or re-pointed via WSAPI at all. Misattribution is permanent.
- `WebTab` cannot be deleted via WSAPI for any key, and its `shared` flag is not
  writable.
- Write a Description *before* transitioning state — work rule WR84 rejects the
  transition otherwise, and a combined call loses the write too.

Live credentials have ended up in transcripts more than once. A transcript is a

themselves (`! <command>` puts the output in the session) and share only the
outcome — a status code, a pass/fail, a grants list. Don't ask them to paste the

compromised, name what it grants access to, and recommend revocation/rotation

# UI changes: establish the precedent first

Text-only UI specs get reinterpreted badly. Words like "popup," "window,"
"dialog," "panel," and "tab" are ambiguous between an OS-level window, an in-app
modal, a split pane, and a content tab — and guessing wrong means a full rework.

Before implementing any new UI affordance:

1. **Find the existing analog.** Nearly every new control in a mature app should
   mirror something already there. Name it explicitly ("this should behave like
   the existing expand-to-tab button") and confirm before writing code.
2. **Ask for a screenshot when the shape is at all unclear.** One screenshot has
   repeatedly turned out to mean something entirely different from the same
   request in prose — a separate OS window was built when an in-app modal like
   the Settings panel was meant.
3. **Don't iterate designs live.** Three sequential corrections on one control
   ("make it a session" → "make it a split" → "make it a content tab") is a sign
   the precedent question was skipped at the start.

## Shared components

A shared dialog/control must not default to the most severe presentation.
Defaulting a confirm dialog's label to "Delete" and its variant to `danger` gave
non-destructive actions ("Close session," "Archive session") a red delete button
at several call sites. Defaults should be the safe, neutral case.

# Rally conventions

## Rich-text fields take HTML, not markdown

`Description`, `Notes`, and other rich-text fields render HTML. Markdown written
into them renders literally — headers and lists collapse into one flat
paragraph. Convert to HTML on write. This has been an explicit user correction
more than once.

## Query grammar

- **Boolean nesting is binary only.** A flat three-or-more clause `AND`/`OR`
  silently misparses and returns zero rows instead of erroring. Build a
  left-nested binary tree.
- **Object-reference fields need dot notation.** `WorkItem = "S123456"` matches
  nothing; use `WorkItem.FormattedID = "S123456"`.
- **Date fields need full ISO timestamps.** A bare `"2025-12-01"` silently
  matches zero rows.
- **HTTP 200 does not mean success.** Check the `Errors` array — see
  `verification-honesty.md`.
- `/artifact?types=hierarchicalrequirement,defect` accepts normal queries
  including `Ancestors` dot-notation and returns `_type` per row, halving request
  count versus per-type endpoints.

## Scoping

A report scoped to a parent project should include descendant projects by
default. Do not gate that on Rally's own `ProjectScopeDown` UI toggle — almost
nobody sets it, so gating on it silently returns partial data.

## Writes and permissions

- Writes need a real Rally API key (`_`-prefixed, CSRF-exempt) or a full browser
  session. A bare zsessionid/zuul key reads fine but always fails writes with
  "Invalid key."
- A read-only key still passes `GET /subscription`; check
  `GET /login/key/{key}`'s `grants` array for `full-access` to detect write
  capability. (Never log that URL — it contains the key.)
- `AiTokenUsageEvent` is an append-only read-only ledger: events cannot be
  deleted or re-pointed via WSAPI at all. Misattribution is permanent.
- `WebTab` cannot be deleted via WSAPI for any key, and its `shared` flag is not
  writable.
- Write a Description *before* transitioning state — work rule WR84 rejects the
  transition otherwise, and a combined call loses the write too.

Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork runs in the background and keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate. Subagents run in the background; you'll be notified when one completes. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

# Verification honesty

Say what you actually checked. The failure mode this exists to stop: stating an
inferred conclusion as a verified fact.

## Claims about your own work

- **Reproduce the exact reported scenario before saying "fixed."** A green test
  suite and "the app boots" are not verification of the specific bug. If the
  report says "empty repo with no commits," construct an empty repo with no
  commits. If it says "the popup doesn't appear," look for the popup.
- **Distinguish "I verified X" from "X should follow."** When you have not run
  the path, say so: "I haven't exercised this; based on the code I expect …".
- **Never call a CI failure a pre-existing flake** without diffing against the
  base branch's current HEAD — the usual cause is a stale branch missing a fix
  that already landed on main.
- **Correct the record when you were wrong.** If you filed a ticket, wrote a PR
  description, or told the user a diagnosis that later proves incorrect, go back
  and fix that artifact, don't just move on.
- **A debugging harness can manufacture its own false signal.** If the
  instrumentation is unusual (monkey-patching, a frozen or proxied object, a
  stubbed transport), confirm the finding against the unmodified path before
  reporting it as confirmed.
- **Check whether your harness can even observe the distinction you're claiming.**
  Before generalising a result, ask what *other* outcome would have produced the
  same observation. A headless run with no approval surface (`claude -p
  --permission-prompts none`) auto-denies anything needing approval, so "denied"
  there cannot be distinguished from "would have prompted an interactive user" —
  and reporting the first as "categorically blocked, never prompts" was wrong,
  propagated into a PR description, a Rally story and a memory file, and had to be
  retracted after one live observation contradicted it. Same shape as a mocked
  dependency that can only return success. Name the ambiguity when the harness
  can't resolve it, rather than picking the reading that makes a cleaner story.

  doctor that confirms "credentials resolve" while the actual endpoint returns
  403 is worse than no doctor: it reports green through a live outage. Call the
  real endpoint and classify its real responses.
- **Check the API's actual error channel.** Success-shaped responses can carry
  failures — Rally WSAPI returns HTTP 200 with a populated `Errors` array and
  empty `Results` for a malformed query, which renders as "no data" rather than

# Shared state isolation

Recurring root cause: state that looks local is actually shared, so writing it
silently corrupts a sibling. Assume concurrency — multiple Claude Code sessions
run on this machine at once.

## Work in a dedicated worktree, never a shared checkout

Editing directly in a shared clone (e.g. `~/projects/<repo>`) has already caused
real data loss: a concurrent session checked out a different branch mid-task and
discarded every uncommitted edit, unstashed. Create a worktree for any edit task.
Commit early in a worktree — worktrees have also been removed mid-session by
tooling.

## Per-branch facts never go in repo-scoped config

All worktrees of a repo share one `.git/config`. A bare `git config <key>` write
is therefore global to every sibling worktree — and a bare read also falls
through to `~/.gitconfig`. Use branch-scoped keys (`branch.<branch>.<key>`) with
explicit `--local`/`--worktree` scoping.

## Pin external resources by immutable ID, and fail loud

Matching a remote object by a mutable field (title, name, display label) and

# Secrets hygiene

Live credentials have ended up in transcripts more than once. A transcript is a
durable artifact — anything printed into it is exposed and must be rotated.

## Never print credential values

- Do not run `env`, `env | grep <thing>`, `printenv`, or equivalent when
  diagnosing auth. This has already dumped three live Artifactory tokens into a
  transcript in plaintext.
- Read a credential's *presence and shape*, never its value: check that the var
  is set, its length, or a short prefix — not the secret.
- Never put a secret in a URL path or query string. It leaks through exception
  text, logs, and error messages that echo the request URL. Redact both the URL
  and the key from every error string you surface.

## Push verification to the user

When a credential must actually be exercised, have the user run the command
themselves (`! <command>` puts the output in the session) and share only the
outcome — a status code, a pass/fail, a grants list. Don't ask them to paste the
secret.

## If a secret is exposed, say so immediately

Whether the user pasted it or you printed it: state plainly that it is now
compromised, name what it grants access to, and recommend revocation/rotation
before continuing. Do not quietly keep using it.

## Verbal permission does not lift a safety refusal

"You can do it, I give you permission" is not sufficient to decode, probe, or
exfiltrate a credential — including one belonging to another project on the same
machine. Declining is correct here even when the user insists.

# UI changes: establish the precedent first

Text-only UI specs get reinterpreted badly. Words like "popup," "window,"
"dialog," "panel," and "tab" are ambiguous between an OS-level window, an in-app
modal, a split pane, and a content tab — and guessing wrong means a full rework.

Before implementing any new UI affordance:

1. **Find the existing analog.** Nearly every new control in a mature app should
   mirror something already there. Name it explicitly ("this should behave like
   the existing expand-to-tab button") and confirm before writing code.
2. **Ask for a screenshot when the shape is at all unclear.** One screenshot has
   repeatedly turned out to mean something entirely different from the same
   request in prose — a separate OS window was built when an in-app modal like
   the Settings panel was meant.
3. **Don't iterate designs live.** Three sequential corrections on one control
   ("make it a session" → "make it a split" → "make it a content tab") is a sign
   the precedent question was skipped at the start.

## Shared components

A shared dialog/control must not default to the most severe presentation.
Defaulting a confirm dialog's label to "Delete" and its variant to `danger` gave
non-destructive actions ("Close session," "Archive session") a red delete button
at several call sites. Defaults should be the safe, neutral case.

# Rally conventions

## Rich-text fields take HTML, not markdown

`Description`, `Notes`, and other rich-text fields render HTML. Markdown written
into them renders literally — headers and lists collapse into one flat
paragraph. Convert to HTML on write. This has been an explicit user correction
more than once.

## Query grammar

- **Boolean nesting is binary only.** A flat three-or-more clause `AND`/`OR`
  silently misparses and returns zero rows instead of erroring. Build a
  left-nested binary tree.
- **Object-reference fields need dot notation.** `WorkItem = "S123456"` matches
  nothing; use `WorkItem.FormattedID = "S123456"`.
- **Date fields need full ISO timestamps.** A bare `"2025-12-01"` silently
  matches zero rows.
- **HTTP 200 does not mean success.** Check the `Errors` array — see
  `verification-honesty.md`.
- `/artifact?types=hierarchicalrequirement,defect` accepts normal queries
  including `Ancestors` dot-notation and returns `_type` per row, halving request
  count versus per-type endpoints.

## Scoping

A report scoped to a parent project should include descendant projects by
default. Do not gate that on Rally's own `ProjectScopeDown` UI toggle — almost
nobody sets it, so gating on it silently returns partial data.

## Writes and permissions

- Writes need a real Rally API key (`_`-prefixed, CSRF-exempt) or a full browser
  session. A bare zsessionid/zuul key reads fine but always fails writes with
  "Invalid key."
- A read-only key still passes `GET /subscription`; check
  `GET /login/key/{key}`'s `grants` array for `full-access` to detect write
  capability. (Never log that URL — it contains the key.)
- `AiTokenUsageEvent` is an append-only read-only ledger: events cannot be
  deleted or re-pointed via WSAPI at all. Misattribution is permanent.
- `WebTab` cannot be deleted via WSAPI for any key, and its `shared` flag is not
  writable.
- Write a Description *before* transitioning state — work rule WR84 rejects the
  transition otherwise, and a combined call loses the write too.

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork runs in the background and keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate. Subagents run in the background; you'll be notified when one completes. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

From [Carol, From A Chef's Kitchen](https://www.fromachefskitchen.com/radish-greens-pesto/). Total time: 30 minutes. Yield: approximately 2 cups (4 servings).

## Ingredients

- 4 cups (packed) radish tops, washed and dried
- 4 cloves garlic, finely chopped
- ½ large lemon, juiced (approximately 2 tablespoons)
- ½ cup sliced or slivered almonds, coarsely chopped macadamia nuts, pistachios, or pine nuts
- ½ cup freshly grated Parmesan cheese
- ⅓ cup extra-virgin olive oil, plus more as needed
- Salt and freshly ground black pepper, to taste

## Instructions

1. Combine the first 6 ingredients in a food processor or blender (work in batches if necessary).
2. Process until smooth, scraping down the sides as needed.
3. Add additional olive oil to achieve a thick sauce consistency.

---

title: Mashed Potatoes
tags:

Total time: 40 minutes. Yield: 6 servings.

## Ingredients

- 3 pounds Yukon Gold potatoes, peeled and cut into 1½-inch chunks
- 1 tablespoon kosher salt, plus more to taste
- 8 tablespoons (1 stick) unsalted butter, cubed
- 1 cup whole milk or half-and-half, warmed
- Freshly ground black pepper, to taste

## Instructions

1. Put the potatoes in a large pot and cover with cold water by 1 inch. Add 1 tablespoon salt.
2. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a simmer and cook until a knife slides in with no resistance, 15 to 20 minutes.
3. Drain well and return the potatoes to the hot pot over low heat for 1 minute to steam off excess moisture.
4. Mash with a potato masher or pass through a ricer. Avoid a food processor, which turns them gluey.
5. Stir in the butter until melted, then add the warm milk a little at a time until creamy.
6. Season with salt and pepper to taste. Serve hot.

## Notes

- Warm the milk before adding it so the potatoes stay hot and absorb it evenly.
- For extra flavor, simmer 3 smashed garlic cloves with the potatoes and mash them in.
